author: Carlos Martinez
title: Eye Strain and Screen Distance: Preventing Fatigue in Long iRacing Sessions
description: How screen distance, monitor size, and viewing angles affect eye fatigue in sim racing. Real solutions I use on my rig to race injury-free for hours.

sections.p: I used to finish a three-hour endurance race with my eyes feeling like sandpaper. The first hour felt fine—then around hour two, I'd notice my vision getting softer, my head drifting closer to the monitor without me realizing it, and a dull ache settling behind my eyes. I'd blame fatigue or the competition intensity, but the real culprit was screen distance and ergonomic carelessness. After adjusting how my cockpit is set up and understanding the geometry of viewing angles, I can now run full-length endurance events without that post-race eye throb. This isn't about having perfect 20/20 vision; it's about respecting how your eyes work during extended focus, and tweaking your rig accordingly.

sections.h2: Why Screen Distance Matters More Than You Think

sections.p: Your eyes have a natural resting focal distance—about 20 inches to infinity—where the muscles around the lens (ciliary muscles) are most relaxed. Stare at something closer than that for hours, and those muscles fatigue. In sim racing, most of us sit roughly 2 to 3 feet from our screen. That's well within the close-focus zone, which means your eyes are under constant accommodation stress.

The problem compounds when your screen is too small relative to that distance. If you're 30 inches away from a 24-inch monitor, your viewing angle is narrow—you're focusing hard on small details like turn-in markers and apex cones. Push back to 36 inches with the same monitor? Same small viewing angle, same eye strain. But move to a 32-inch or widen your monitor setup at that distance? Suddenly the image fills more of your peripheral vision, your eyes can track motion more naturally, and you're not locked into such intense convergence.

sections.tip: The 20-20-20 rule applies even in racing: every 20 minutes, look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds. I set a quiet phone alert during practice sessions to remind me. Sounds silly until you realize those 20-second breaks drop my post-session eye fatigue by roughly 40%.

sections.h2: Finding Your Ideal Viewing Distance and Monitor Size

sections.p: There's no universal 'correct' distance—it depends on your monitor size, cockpit depth, and how close you naturally want to sit. But there are guides. Many ergonomics sources suggest an arm's length (roughly 24 to 26 inches) as baseline, though sim racers often sit further back because we're not typing.

On my aluminum cockpit, I sit about 32 to 36 inches from a 27-inch 1440p 120 Hz monitor. That gives me a viewing angle of roughly 40 to 45 degrees—enough to see track markers and traffic without cramping my eyes, but not so wide that I'm missing detail. If I owned a 32-inch or ultrawide, I'd push back to 40 inches or more; if I were using a 24-inch, I'd move closer, maybe 26 to 28 inches, to keep that viewing angle consistent.

list: 24-inch monitor: 24–28 inches away (~90-100 degree total viewing angle)
27-inch monitor: 28–36 inches away (~80-90 degree viewing angle)
32-inch monitor or ultrawide: 36–42 inches away (~70-80 degree viewing angle)
Triple monitor setup: 28–32 inches away from center screen (total ~120-135 degrees)

sections.p: The goal is that the entire screen fills your comfortable natural field of view without you having to physically turn your head or eyes to extreme angles. Anything tighter than that, and you're forcing accommodation. Anything looser, and you'll creep forward during an intense session without noticing.

sections.h2: Monitor Height, Angle, and Vertical Strain

sections.p: Horizontal distance is only half the equation. Monitor height and tilt angle matter enormously. Your eyes naturally prefer to gaze downward—about 15 to 20 degrees below horizontal is where the ciliary muscles are least fatigued. If your monitor is level with your eyes or angled upward, you're either tilting your head back (neck strain) or forcing your eyes up (more muscle fatigue).

On my cockpit, I have my monitor tilted up slightly at the base—roughly 10 to 15 degrees—so that the center of the screen sits about 15 to 20 degrees below my eye level when I'm seated. This feels natural and keeps my neck neutral. If your rig allows it, mount your monitor on an adjustable arm or tilt-mount, then experiment. Raise it until your head naturally falls into a comfortable position, then measure from there.

sections.tip: After adjusting monitor height, give yourself at least two full practice sessions before racing. Neck and eye positioning feels 'wrong' for a while because your muscles are resetting their baseline. Trust the ergonomics, not your immediate comfort sensation.

sections.h2: Blue Light, Refresh Rate, and Visual Stability

sections.p: Higher refresh rates reduce eye strain during panning motion. At 60 Hz, motion across the screen feels slightly stuttery, which forces your eyes to work harder to track it smoothly. At 120 Hz or higher (which I run on my 1440p monitor), motion feels fluid, and your visual system doesn't have to compensate as aggressively. This compounds over hours.

Blue light itself isn't the enemy—blue light exposure from screens isn't proven to cause permanent damage. But if you race in a dark room without ambient lighting, the contrast between your bright screen and the dark cockpit can increase pupil oscillation and fatigue. I keep my rig area lit with indirect LED strips at roughly 30 to 50% intensity. It's enough to reduce the ambient contrast without creating glare or reflections on the screen.

sections.h2: Practical Tweaks You Can Make This Week

olist: Measure your current screen distance. Sit naturally in your cockpit, and measure from your eyes to the center of the monitor. Write it down.
Calculate your viewing angle using the monitor size and distance. (Rough formula: viewing angle ≈ 2 × arctan(monitor width ÷ 2 ÷ distance).) Aim for 70–90 degrees.
Adjust monitor height so the center sits 15–20 degrees below your natural eye level when seated. Use a monitor arm or shims if needed.
Add ambient lighting to your cockpit—even a small LED strip reduces contrast-related fatigue.
Set a phone alarm for every 20 minutes during practice. When it goes off, look away at something distant for 20 seconds.
If you wear glasses, ensure your prescription is optimized for intermediate distance (roughly 2–4 feet), not close-up reading. Tell your optometrist you stare at a screen 3 feet away for hours.

sections.p: The MOZA R9 wheelbase and CRP2 pedals are rock-solid for force feedback and consistency, but they don't help you position your head correctly. That's entirely on your cockpit geometry. Spend an afternoon getting this right, and you'll notice the difference in your fifth consecutive hour of racing, not your first.

sections.h2: When to Suspect a Deeper Issue

sections.p: If you've adjusted distance, height, and lighting, but eye strain persists—especially if it's accompanied by blurred vision, double vision, or persistent headaches—that's a sign to see an optometrist. Some people have convergence insufficiency (eyes don't align properly at near distance) or astigmatism that becomes apparent only during prolonged focus. A quick exam can rule that out and save you months of discomfort.

Also consider dry eyes. Sim racing concentrates your attention so intensely that you blink less—studies show blink rate drops by 20–30% during focused screen tasks. Your tears evaporate faster. If your eyes feel gritty or watery (paradoxically, dry eyes cause tearing), use artificial tears before and after sessions. It sounds basic, but it's often the overlooked factor.

faqs.q: Is 27 inches the best size for a sim racing monitor?
faqs.a: Not universally. A 27-inch at 32–36 inches distance works well for most setups, but it depends on your cockpit depth and visual preference. If you sit further back (40+ inches), a 32-inch or ultrawide is more comfortable. If you're closer (24–28 inches), a 24-inch might be better. Prioritize viewing angle (70–90 degrees) over picking a specific inch size.

faqs.q: Does 120 Hz really reduce eye strain compared to 60 Hz?
faqs.a: Yes, noticeably. Higher refresh rates make motion smoother, which reduces the effort your eyes spend tracking. Over a three-hour race, the cumulative fatigue difference is real. That said, a properly positioned 60 Hz screen will cause less strain than a poorly positioned 144 Hz screen, so distance and height come first.

faqs.q: Should I wear blue-light blocking glasses while racing?
faqs.a: They don't hurt, but they're not necessary. The bigger factors are distance, monitor height, ambient lighting, and blink rate. If you already wear glasses and your optometrist recommends blue-light coatings, fine—but don't buy them as a standalone solution for eye strain. Fix your setup geometry first.

faqs.q: How do I know if I'm sitting too close to the screen?
faqs.a: If you catch yourself leaning forward after 30 minutes, or if your eyes feel fatigued after an hour even when you're not racing intensely, you're likely too close. Also, if small details (like apex markers) feel unclear without being blurry, your viewing angle is too narrow. Push back 3–4 inches and reassess after a full practice session.
